entry: Ancient [[Algorithm|algorithm]] for finding all [[Prime number|prime numbers]] up to a given limit. It works by iteratively marking the multiples of each prime, starting with 2, as composite; the numbers left unmarked are the primes. Unlike trial division, it uses only additions, with no multiplications or divisions. The earliest known reference, in Nicomachus of Gerasa's *Introduction to Arithmetic* (an early 2nd-century CE book), attributes it to [[Eratosthenes|Eratosthenes of Cyrene]], a 3rd-century BCE Greek mathematician. It is one of the most efficient ways to find all smaller primes and can be used to find primes in arithmetic progressions.

[[International System of Units|SI]] derived unit of equivalent dose of [[Ionizing radiation]], named after Swedish medical physicist Rolf Maximilian Sievert. It measures the stochastic health risk of radiation, defined as the probability of causing radiation-induced cancer and genetic damage, and is central to dosimetry and radiation protection. Equivalent dose is the absorbed dose, in [[Gray (unit)|grays]], multiplied by a radiation weighting factor that ranges from 1 for photons and electrons to 20 for [[Alpha particle|alpha particles]]. One sievert equals one joule per kilogram but denotes a biological effect rather than a physical quantity. It equals 100 rem, an older unit. The International Commission on Radiological Protection estimates that one sievert results in a 5.5% probability of eventually developing fatal cancer, based on the linear no-threshold model, which is disputed. Natural background radiation averages about 3 millisieverts (mSv) a year.

Luxembourg monarch, King of Hungary from 1387 and Holy Roman Emperor (1433–1437). The son of [[Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor|Charles IV]] and Elizabeth of Pomerania, he gained the Hungarian crown through his marriage to Mary, Queen of Hungary, and was elected King of the Romans in 1410. He was also king of [[Bohemia]] from 1419. He led the Crusade of Nicopolis in 1396 but was decisively defeated by the [[Ottoman Empire]], after which he founded the Order of the Dragon to fight the Turks. He was a driving force behind the Council of Constance (1414–18), which ended the Papal Schism; the council also saw the execution of [[Jan Hus]] despite his initial protection, and it led to the [[Hussite Wars]] that dominated his later life. He sought to reform the empire and the Church together, but the extinction of the Luxembourg male line left this unfulfilled. He was the last male member of the House of Luxembourg.

King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1587–1632) and, as Sigismund, King of Sweden (1592–1599). The first Polish sovereign of the House of Vasa, he was zealously Catholic and imposed Catholicism across his realm. He granted privileges to the [[Jesuits]], whom he employed as advisers and spies during the [[Counter-Reformation]]. He sought absolute power and often undermined parliament. His invasion of Russia during the Time of Troubles led to the seizure of Smolensk and the occupation of Moscow, the greatest territorial extent in Poland's history. In 1596 he moved the capital from [[Kraków]] to [[Warsaw]]. He was deposed as King of Sweden in 1599 after a war led by his uncle, Charles IX. He remains a controversial figure in Poland: his patronage of the arts and architecture and his military victories are weighed against intrigues, religious conflicts and the cession of Ducal Prussia to Brandenburg. Sigismund's Column in Warsaw, the first secular column monument of modern history, was commissioned by his son, Władysław IV Vasa.

Natural language that conveys meaning through the visual-manual modality rather than spoken words. Sign languages combine manual articulation with non-manual markers such as facial expression, and have their own [[Grammar|grammar]] and lexicon. They are distinct from [[Body language|body language]]. They are not universal and are usually not mutually intelligible, although similarities exist. Each country generally has its own native sign language; the 2021 edition of Ethnologue lists 150, while the SIGN-HUB Atlas of Sign Language Structures lists over 200. As of 2021, Indo-Pakistani Sign Language is the most widely used. Sign languages form the core of local Deaf cultures wherever deaf communities exist, and hearing people also use them, such as children of deaf adults. One of the earliest written records is in [[Plato]]'s *Cratylus*, from the fifth century BC. American Sign Language in the [[United States]] and British Sign Language in the [[United Kingdom]] are mutually unintelligible.

Process of varying one or more properties of a periodic waveform to transmit information. In electronics and telecommunication, a message signal, such as sound from a [[Microphone]], video from a camera or a stream of binary digits, is encoded onto a carrier wave. Carriers are needed when the message frequency is too low to transmit practically, since receiving a radio wave requires an antenna about one-quarter of its wavelength. Modulation also lets many channels share one medium through frequency-division multiplexing, as in [[Cable television]]. Analog modulation varies the carrier's amplitude (AM) or frequency (FM) and is used in radio broadcasting. Digital methods include amplitude shift keying, frequency shift keying, phase shift keying, which is used in [[Wi-Fi]], Bluetooth and cellular networks, and quadrature amplitude modulation. Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing, which spreads data across closely spaced sub-carriers, is widely used in WLAN and LTE systems.

[[Electrical engineering]] subfield that analyzes, modifies and synthesizes signals such as sound, images and scientific measurements. Its techniques optimize transmission and digital storage, correct distorted signals, improve subjective video quality and detect components of interest in a measured signal. Its principles are traced to classical numerical analysis of the 17th century, with digital refinements in control systems of the 1940s and 1950s. In 1948, [[Claude Shannon]] published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", which laid groundwork for information communication systems. The field matured in the 1960s and 1970s, and digital signal processing became widespread with specialized processor chips in the 1980s. Analog processing uses circuits such as passive and active filters, while digital processing runs on [[Computer|general-purpose computers]], application-specific chips or [[Field-programmable gate array|field-programmable gate arrays]]. Typical operations include [[Convolution]], multiplication and addition.

Measure of the level of a desired signal relative to background [[Noise|noise]], usually expressed in [[Decibel|decibels]]. It is defined as the ratio of signal power to noise power, and a ratio above 1:1 (greater than 0 dB) indicates more signal than noise. SNR is a key parameter for communication systems, audio equipment, [[Radar|radar]], imaging and data acquisition systems. A high SNR means a signal is clear and easy to detect, while a low SNR means the signal is obscured or corrupted. It can be improved by increasing signal strength, reducing noise, filtering or using error-correction techniques. The Shannon–Hartley theorem, a fundamental law of information theory, shows that the maximum data rate of a channel depends on its bandwidth and SNR. In decibels, SNR (dB) = 10 log₁₀(signal power ÷ noise power).

American actress known for science fiction and action roles. Born in [[New York City]] to television executive Pat Weaver and English actress Elizabeth Inglis, she played Ellen Ripley in the *Alien* films from 1979. Her performance in *Aliens* (1986) earned an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination for Best Actress. She won two Golden Globes in 1989 for *Gorillas in the Mist* and *Working Girl*, and a British Academy Film Award for *The Ice Storm* (1997). Other roles include the *Ghostbusters* films, the *Avatar* series, and voice roles in [[Pixar]]'s *WALL-E* and *Finding Dory*.

Regional power based in the [[Punjab]] region of [[South Asia]], existing from 1799 until 1849. In 1799 Maharaja Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl captured [[Lahore]] from the Sikh triumvirate, and by 1813 he had annexed the other Sikh misls. Afghan influence east of the Indus ended after the fall of Multan in 1818, and in the following decades Durrani Afghans lost Kashmir and Peshawar to the Sikhs. At its peak, the empire extended from Gilgit and Tibet to the deserts of Sindh and from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej, divided into eight provinces. Ranjit Singh modernized the army with European-trained officers and artillery. The empire was religiously diverse and was the last major region of the subcontinent to be conquered by the [[British Empire]]. After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839, the [[East India Company]] exploited internal divisions; the state was annexed after the Second Anglo-Sikh War in 1849.

State in northeastern India, bordering [[Bhutan]], the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] and [[Nepal]]. The Namgyal dynasty founded the Kingdom of Sikkim in the 17th century, ruled by Buddhist priest-kings called the Chogyal. It became a princely state of British India in 1890. After a 1975 referendum, the monarchy was dissolved and Sikkim became India's 22nd state. It contains [[Kangchenjunga]], India's highest peak. Almost 35% of the state is covered by Khangchendzonga National Park, a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. Its economy depends on agriculture and tourism, and the predominant religion is [[Hinduism]], with a significant [[Vajrayana]] Buddhist minority.

Four-bladed, twin-engine, medium-lift military utility helicopter made by Sikorsky Aircraft. Selected in 1976 by the U.S. Army after a fly-off against the Boeing Vertol YUH-61, it entered service in 1979 to replace the Bell UH-1 Iroquois. It is named after the Sauk leader Black Hawk. Variants include the Navy's SH-60 Seahawk, the Air Force's HH-60 Pave Hawk, the Coast Guard's MH-60 Jayhawk and the civilian S-70. The helicopter has been used in combat in [[Afghanistan]] and [[Iraq]], and has been exported to more than 30 countries.

[[Medication]] used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension, sold as Viagra. It works by blocking phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5), an enzyme that breaks down cGMP, which regulates blood flow in the penis, and it requires sexual arousal to work. Pfizer discovered it in 1989 while seeking an angina treatment; it was approved in 1998. Common side effects include headache, heartburn and flushed skin. Caution is advised in people with [[Cardiovascular disease]], and combining it with nitrates such as nitroglycerin can cause a serious drop in [[Blood pressure]]. Rare serious effects include vision problems, hearing loss and priapism.

Demographic cohort following the Greatest Generation and preceding the [[Baby boomers|baby boomers]], generally defined as people born from 1928 to 1945. Low birthrates during the Great Depression and [[World War II]] made it comparatively small in the United States; it includes most who fought in the [[Korean War]]. As young adults its members were often seen as conformist, the "silent majority", yet they also led the civil rights movement and the 1960s counterculture and created rock and roll. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine first used the term in a 1951 article. The United States had 23 million members as of 2019.

Japanese survival horror video game franchise, published by Konami and set mainly in a fictional American town plagued by the supernatural and a cult. The first four games (1999–2004) were developed by Team Silent, a Japanese team within Konami, and received critical acclaim. Later games by Western studios drew much less positive reviews. *P.T.*, a 2014 release that revealed the canceled *Silent Hills* by [[Hideo Kojima|Kojima]] Productions, was also critically acclaimed, but the franchise then went dormant for nearly ten years. Konami revived it in 2022. The games have collectively sold over 19.2 million copies.

Environmental science book by [[Rachel Carson]], published on September 27, 1962. It documented the environmental harm caused by the indiscriminate use of [[DDT]], a pesticide used by soldiers during [[World War II]]. Carson's project was prompted by a 1957 fire ant eradication program that involved aerial spraying of DDT on private land, and by a 1958 letter describing bird deaths after spraying. She accused the [[Chemical industry|chemical industry]] of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its marketing claims unquestioningly. The book drew fierce opposition from chemical companies, but it swayed public opinion, contributed to a reversal in US pesticide policy and a nationwide ban on DDT for agricultural uses, and fueled the environmental movement that led to the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. Critics argue that its emphasis on pesticide risks understated DDT's value in controlling malaria.

Motion picture without synchronized recorded sound, relying on visual storytelling and intertitles. The term is a retronym and something of a misnomer, since films were almost always accompanied by live music from a pianist, theater organist or [[Orchestra|orchestra]], and sometimes a narrator. The silent era ran from the 1890s to the 1920s in most countries. Synchronized dialogue became practical in the 1920s with the Audion amplifier tube and the Vitaphone system, and early sound films such as [[The Jazz Singer]] (1927) were called "talkies". Sound-era films like [[Charlie Chaplin]]'s *City Lights* (1931) kept a music-only soundtrack. [[Thomas Edison]] introduced the kinetoscope as a silent viewer in 1893. Most early motion pictures are lost because nitrate film stock decayed and was flammable, and it is often claimed that around 75 percent of US silent films are lost, though the figure cannot be verified.

Historical region of Central Europe, lying mostly within [[Poland]] with small parts in the [[Czech Republic]] and [[Germany]]. It spans 40,000 sq km and has about 8,000,000 inhabitants. It divides into Lower Silesia, with capital [[Wrocław]], and Upper Silesia. Most of it was annexed by Prussia from Austria in 1742 and became part of the German Empire in 1871. After World War I, parts returned to Poland after insurrections and a plebiscite. In 1945 most German-held Silesia was transferred to Poland under the Potsdam Agreement. Forced population shifts of 1945–48 mean today's inhabitants speak the national languages of their countries.

Polyatomic anion containing silicon and oxygen, or a salt or ester of one. In most silicates a silicon atom sits at the center of a tetrahedron of four oxygen atoms, and these strong, rigid linkages give the rock-like silicates their properties. Tetrahedra link into isolated units such as [[Olivine]], single chains such as [[Pyroxene]], double chains such as amphiboles, sheets such as [[Mica]], and three-dimensional frameworks such as [[Quartz]] and feldspars. Silicate minerals are the largest group of rock-forming minerals, estimated to make up 90 to 95 percent of Earth's crust by volume. Artificial silicates include Portland [[Cement|cement]], [[Ceramic|ceramics]] and [[Glass|glass]]. Silicates with alkali cations, such as sodium metasilicate, are fairly soluble in water.

Region in [[California|Northern California]] that is the first global center for high technology and innovation, located in Santa Clara County and southern San Mateo County. It was there that the silicon-based [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]], the microprocessor and the microcomputer were developed. Today it is home to many leading high-tech corporations, including the headquarters of more than 30 Fortune 1000 businesses, and thousands of startups, such as [[Google|Alphabet (Google)]], [[Intel]], [[Netflix]] and [[Nvidia]]. [[Stanford University]]'s leadership was especially important in its early development. Journalist Don Hoefler popularized the name in a 1971 article. The Bay Area accounts for one-third of US venture capital investment, and as of 2015 San Jose's metropolitan area had the third-highest GDP per capita in the world, after [[Zurich]] and Oslo.

Hard chemical compound of silicon and carbon, also known as carborundum, and a wide-bandgap [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]]. Mass-produced as powder and crystals since 1893 for use as an abrasive, it is sintered into very hard ceramics for high-endurance uses such as disc brakes, [[Clutch|clutches]] and ballistic plates in [[Bulletproof vest|bulletproof vests]]. It is used in semiconductor devices that operate at high temperatures or voltages. Electronic uses such as [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]] and early radio detectors were first demonstrated around 1907. Naturally occurring moissanite is extremely rare, found in certain meteorites, and virtually all silicon carbide sold is synthetic.

Oxide of silicon, also known as silica, with the chemical formula SiO₂. Commonly found in nature as [[Quartz|quartz]], it is the major constituent of [[Sand|sand]] and of most [[Glass|glass]]. In most forms each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. Crystalline forms include quartz, tridymite, cristobalite, stishovite and coesite, while amorphous forms include [[Opal|opal]] and diatomaceous earth. Alpha quartz is the most stable form at room temperature, and its abrupt change to beta-quartz at 573 °C can fracture ceramics or rock. Silica is used in microelectronics and in food and pharmaceutical products.

Polymer composed of repeating siloxane units, with an inorganic silicon–oxygen backbone and organic groups attached to the silicon. Silicones are typically colorless oils or rubber-like substances, used in sealants, adhesives, lubricants, medicine, cookware, thermal insulation and electrical insulation. They are often confused with [[Silicon|silicon]], a hard gray solid used in integrated circuits and solar cells, but silicones are usually electrical insulators. F. S. Kipping coined the word in 1901 for a polymer he noted was unlike the ketone benzophenone, so siloxane is now the preferred term. Many silicones are crosslinked, which gives them a rubbery or hard texture. Some consumer caulks cure more slowly by releasing [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]], the acid in [[Vinegar|vinegar]]. The industry was launched in the 1930s, and James Franklin Hyde is credited as the "Father of Silicones."

Natural protein fiber, most often produced by the larvae of insects to form cocoons. Silk is composed mainly of fibroin (75–80%), with a coating of sericin (20–25%). The best-known silk comes from the cocoons of the mulberry silkworm [[Bombyx mori]], which is reared in captivity in sericulture. Many other insects, including bees, wasps, ants and beetles, produce silk, as do [[Spider|spiders]] and other arachnids. Silk fabric was first developed in ancient China, where silk protein has been found in soil from the Neolithic site of Jiahu, dating back about 8,500 years. Silk production stayed confined to China until the [[Silk Road]] trade routes opened, and China kept a virtual monopoly for another thousand years. Commercial silk is unraveled as one continuous thread from cocoons whose pupae are killed before the moths emerge. Today silk remains integral to high-end [[Textile|textiles]], medical sutures and emerging biomaterials, although synthetic alternatives exist.

Structure for storing bulk materials, such as grain, coal, [[Cement|cement]], carbon black, woodchips or sawdust. The word derives from Ancient Greek *sirós*, "pit for holding grain." Three types are in widespread use: tower silos, bunker silos and bag silos. Storage silos are cylindrical, typically 10 to 90 ft (3 to 27 m) in diameter and 30 to 275 ft (10 to 90 m) high, and may be built of wood staves, concrete or [[Steel|steel]] panels. Concrete stave silos are made from precast blocks locked together and held by steel hoops, tightened more closely toward the bottom, where pressure is greatest. Low-oxygen silos keep contents in a low-oxygen atmosphere to preserve quality. In agriculture, silos store silage, a [[Fermentation|fermented]] feed. The tower silo was invented by Franklin Hiram King.
